Q49. Electromagnet: (i) Made of soft iron, retains magnetism only while current flows. (ii) Strength and polarity can be changed. Permanent magnet: (i) Made of steel, retains magnetism permanently without needing current. (ii) Strength and polarity cannot be changed easily.

Official Answer

Q50. Soft iron is used because it is easily magnetised and demagnetised. When current flows, it gets quickly magnetised and attracts the armature. When current stops (contact breaks), it instantly loses its magnetism, allowing the armature to spring back. Steel cannot be used as it would retain magnetism and hold the armature permanently.

Official Answer

Q51. Fleming's left-hand rule: Hold the left hand so that the forefinger, the middle finger and the thumb are mutually perpendicular. If the forefinger points in the direction of the magnetic field (B) and the middle finger points in the direction of the current (I), then the thumb points in the direction of the force (motion) on the conductor.

Official Answer

Q52. The force F = BIl depends on: (1) Strength of magnetic field B — greater the B, greater the force (F ∝ B). (2) Current I in the conductor — greater the current, greater the force (F ∝ I). (3) Length l of the conductor in the field — greater the length, greater the force (F ∝ l).

Official Answer

Q53. (a) Zero: when the current in the conductor is in the direction of the magnetic field (or parallel/anti-parallel to it), angle between them = 0° or 180°. (b) Maximum: when the current in the conductor is normal (perpendicular) to the magnetic field, angle = 90°.

Official Answer

Q54. First law: Whenever there is a change in the magnetic flux linked with a coil, an e.m.f. (and hence a current) is induced in it. The induced e.m.f. lasts as long as the change in magnetic flux continues. Second law: The magnitude of the induced e.m.f. is directly proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linked with the coil: e = N × (ΔΦ/Δt), where N is the number of turns.

Official Answer

Q55. Lenz's law: The direction of the induced current in a coil is always such as to oppose the change in the magnetic flux that causes the induced current. The induced current must oppose the change because of conservation of energy. If the induced current aided the change, it would cause greater change and thus greater current — this would go on indefinitely, creating energy from nothing, violating conservation of energy. The opposing effect means mechanical work must be done to overcome the opposition, and this work appears as electrical energy in the circuit.

Official Answer

Q56. Fleming's right-hand rule: Stretch the thumb, the forefinger and the middle finger of the right hand mutually perpendicular to each other. If the forefinger points in the direction of the magnetic field (B) and the thumb points in the direction of motion of the conductor, then the middle finger points in the direction of the induced current (e.m.f.).

Official Answer

Q57. (1) Eddy current loss (Iron loss): Electric currents are induced in the iron core due to changing flux, causing heating. Minimised by using a laminated core of thin insulated sheets. (2) Copper loss (Resistance heating): Current flowing through the resistance of the primary and secondary coils produces heat (I²R loss). Minimised by using thick copper wires. (Other losses: hysteresis loss, flux leakage.)

Official Answer

Q58. For an ideal (100% efficient) transformer, input power = output power. Therefore, Vp × Ip = Vs × Is. Assumption: The transformer is ideal, meaning there are no energy losses (no eddy currents, no resistance in coils, no flux leakage, no hysteresis loss).

Official Answer

Q59. The iron core is laminated to reduce eddy current losses. In a solid iron core, large eddy currents would be induced by the changing magnetic flux, causing significant heat generation and energy loss. Thin insulated laminations increase the resistance of the paths for eddy currents, reducing their magnitude and thus minimising energy loss.

Official Answer

Official Answer

Q63. The diagram shows a circular current-carrying loop passing through a cardboard. Three field lines are drawn: (1) at the point P where current goes up — anticlockwise concentric circles, (2) at point Q where current goes down — clockwise concentric circles, (3) at the centre — the field line passes along the axis of the loop. The two factors on which the magnitude of the magnetic field at the centre depends are: (i) the strength of current in the loop — greater the current, greater the field; (ii) the radius of the loop — smaller the radius, greater the field at the centre.

Q64. A solenoid is a long cylindrical coil of wire. Inside the solenoid, magnetic field lines are nearly straight, parallel to the axis and uniformly spaced (uniform field). Outside the solenoid, the field lines are similar to those of a bar magnet — they emerge from the N pole and re-enter at the S pole. The end where current flows anticlockwise is the North pole; the end where current flows clockwise is the South pole. The field is much stronger inside than outside the solenoid.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q65. An electromagnet consists of a soft iron bar AB wound with insulated copper wire connected to a battery, a rheostat, and a key (switch). Current from the battery passes through the coil. The end where current flows anticlockwise is the North pole (N) and the end where current flows clockwise is the South pole (S). Precaution: The source of current must be d.c. (direct current), not a.c., to maintain constant polarity.

Official Answer

Q66. A D.C. motor consists of: (1) Armature coil (ABCD) — a rectangular coil of insulated copper wire that rotates. (2) Strong permanent magnet (N and S poles) — provides the magnetic field. (3) Split ring commutator — two halves of a split copper ring, one attached to each end of the coil. (4) Carbon brushes — press against the commutator, connecting the coil to the external circuit.

Working: When direct current is passed through the coil via the brushes and commutator, the sides AB and CD of the coil experience forces in opposite directions (by Fleming's left-hand rule). This creates a couple (torque) that rotates the coil. After half a rotation, the commutator reverses the direction of current through the coil, so the torque continues to act in the same direction, maintaining continuous rotation.

Function of commutator: It reverses the direction of current through the coil after each half rotation, ensuring that the torque always acts in the same direction, enabling continuous rotation of the coil.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q67. (a) The coil experiences a torque due to the forces on its current-carrying arms in the magnetic field, causing it to rotate. (b) The coil will come to rest when its plane becomes normal (perpendicular) to the magnetic field — at this position the coil is in stable equilibrium. (c) (i) The couple is maximum when the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field (i.e., initial position). (ii) The couple is minimum (zero) when the plane of the coil is normal to the magnetic field. (d) D.C. motor (also: galvanometer).

Official Answer

Q68. Principle: A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force (F = BIl). When a coil carrying current is placed in a magnetic field, the forces on its opposite sides form a couple that rotates the coil.

Construction: (1) Armature — a rectangular coil ABCD wound on a soft iron core. (2) Field magnets — a strong horseshoe or U-shaped permanent magnet providing a radial magnetic field. (3) Split ring commutator — two half-rings attached to the two ends of the armature coil; they rotate with the coil. (4) Brushes — two carbon brushes press against the commutator halves, maintaining sliding electrical contact with the external circuit.

Working: When d.c. is supplied through the brushes, current flows through the coil. By Fleming's left-hand rule, side AB experiences a downward force and side CD experiences an upward force (or vice versa). This creates a torque that rotates the coil. After half a rotation, the commutator half-rings exchange brushes, reversing the current direction in the coil so that the same sides always experience the same direction of force, maintaining continuous rotation in the same direction.

Energy conversion: Electrical energy → Mechanical energy.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q69. Experiment: Connect a coil of several turns to a centre-zero galvanometer G. Hold a bar magnet NS near the coil. (i) When the north pole of the magnet is pushed into the coil, the galvanometer deflects, showing that a current is induced. The deflection is momentary and lasts only as long as the magnet is moving. (ii) When the magnet is held stationary inside the coil, no deflection is observed. (iii) When the north pole is pulled out of the coil, the galvanometer deflects in the opposite direction.

Faraday's law: Whenever there is a change in the magnetic flux linked with a coil, an e.m.f. is induced in it; the magnitude of the induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux: e = N(ΔΦ/Δt).

Lenz's law: The direction of the induced current is always such as to oppose the change in magnetic flux that caused it. When the north pole approaches, the induced current creates a north pole at the near end of the coil to repel the approaching magnet. When the north pole moves away, the near end becomes a south pole to attract and oppose the withdrawal.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q70. Principle: Electromagnetic induction — when a coil rotates in a magnetic field, the magnetic flux linked with it changes continuously, inducing an alternating e.m.f.

Construction: (1) Armature coil — a rectangular coil ABCD mounted on an axle, free to rotate between the poles of a magnet. (2) Field magnets — strong permanent magnets (N and S poles) providing the magnetic field. (3) Slip rings — two conducting rings attached to the two ends of the armature coil; they rotate with the coil. (4) Carbon brushes — press against the slip rings, connected to the external circuit.

Working: As the coil rotates, the sides AB and CD cut through the magnetic field lines alternately. By Fleming's right-hand rule, e.m.f. is induced in each side alternately in different directions as the coil rotates. When the coil plane is parallel to the field, the sides cut field lines at maximum rate, giving maximum e.m.f. When the coil plane is perpendicular to the field, sides move parallel to field lines, giving zero e.m.f. After a full rotation, the cycle repeats, producing alternating current.

Frequency: The frequency of a.c. equals the number of complete rotations of the coil per second (n rotations per second = n Hz frequency).

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q71. Principle: Electromagnetic induction (mutual induction).

Construction: A step-up transformer consists of (1) a primary coil with a smaller number of turns of thick wire, (2) a secondary coil with a larger number of turns of thin wire, and (3) a soft iron laminated core on which both coils are wound.

Working: When alternating current flows through the primary coil, it creates a changing magnetic flux in the soft iron core. This changing flux links with the secondary coil and induces an alternating e.m.f. in it. Since the secondary has more turns than the primary (Ns > Np), the induced e.m.f. in the secondary (Vs) is greater than the primary voltage (Vp): Vs/Vp = Ns/Np > 1. Energy is conserved, so the secondary current is less than the primary current.

Characteristics of primary coil compared to secondary: (i) The primary coil has fewer turns than the secondary. (ii) The wire of the primary coil is thicker (lower resistance) than the secondary wire, since it carries more current.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q72. By Lenz's law, the induced current always flows in a direction that opposes the cause producing it. For example, when a north pole of a magnet approaches a coil, the induced current creates a north pole at the near end of the coil to repel the approaching magnet. This means that work must be done against this repulsive force to move the magnet toward the coil. The mechanical work done in overcoming the opposition is converted into electrical energy (the induced current). If instead the induced current aided the motion, energy would be created from nothing — violating conservation of energy. Therefore, Lenz's law is a consequence of energy conservation.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q73. Similarities: (1) Both have an armature coil that rotates between the poles of a magnet. (2) Both use carbon brushes to make electrical contact with the rotating coil.

Dissimilarities:
D.C. Motor — (1) It converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. (2) It uses a split ring commutator to maintain unidirectional rotation.
A.C. Generator — (1) It converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. (2) It uses slip rings (not a split ring commutator) to output alternating current.

Official Answer

Q74. Step-up transformer: (1) It increases the voltage: Vs > Vp. (2) Number of turns in secondary > number of turns in primary (Ns > Np). (3) Secondary current is less than primary current.

Step-down transformer: (1) It decreases the voltage: Vs < Vp. (2) Number of turns in secondary < number of turns in primary (Ns < Np). (3) Secondary current is greater than primary current. The secondary coil wire is thicker.

Official Answer

Q75. (i) Power generating station: Step-up transformer — it steps up the voltage from the generator to a very high value (e.g., 11 kV to 132 kV or 400 kV) for long-distance transmission, thereby reducing current and minimising energy losses due to resistance heating (I²R). (ii) Power sub-station: Step-down transformer — it steps down the high transmission voltage to a safe, usable level (e.g., 230 V for homes) before supplying to consumers.

Official Answer

Q76. (a) The frequency of the output voltage is doubled. Reason: Frequency equals the number of complete rotations per second. If the speed is doubled, the coil completes twice as many rotations per second, so the frequency doubles. (b) The maximum output voltage (peak e.m.f.) is also doubled. Reason: The rate at which the coil cuts magnetic field lines doubles when the speed doubles, so the rate of change of flux doubles, and by Faraday's law, the induced e.m.f. doubles.

Official Answer

E. Numericals

Q77. Given: N = 100 turns, ΔΦ = 5 mWb − 0 = 5 × 10⁻³ Wb, Δt = 5 s

Formula: e = N × (ΔΦ/Δt)
e = 100 × (5 × 10⁻³ / 5)
e = 100 × 1 × 10⁻³
e = 0.1 V = 100 mV

The induced e.m.f. = 100 mV.

Official Answer

Q78. Given: Np = 800, Ns = 8, Vp = 220 V

Formula: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np
Vs = Vp × (Ns/Np) = 220 × (8/800) = 220 × (1/100)
Vs = 2.2 V

The output voltage = 2.2 V. (This is a step-down transformer.)

Official Answer

Q79. Given: Vp = 240 V, Vs = 8 V, Np = 4800 turns

Formula: Ns/Np = Vs/Vp
Ns = Np × (Vs/Vp) = 4800 × (8/240) = 4800 × (1/30)
Ns = 160 turns

The secondary coil has 160 turns.

Official Answer

Q80. Given: Vp = 220 V, Vs = 44 V, Is = 2 A

(a) Turns ratio Np : Ns = Vp : Vs = 220 : 44 = 5 : 1
Turns ratio = 5 : 1 (or 1:5 for Ns:Np)

(b) For an ideal transformer, input power = output power:
Vp × Ip = Vs × Is
220 × Ip = 44 × 2
220 × Ip = 88
Ip = 88/220 = 0.4 A

The input current = 0.4 A.

Official Answer

Force at θ = 60°:

Current = 6 A; Force at 60° ≈ 0.65 N.

Q99. Given: N = 200 turns, Φ1 = 1.5 × 10⁻² Wb, Φ2 = 3.5 × 10⁻² Wb, Δt = 0.2 s

Change in flux: ΔΦ = 3.5 × 10⁻² − 1.5 × 10⁻² = 2.0 × 10⁻² Wb

(a) Rate of change per turn = ΔΦ/Δt = (2.0 × 10⁻²)/0.2 = 0.1 Wb/s = 0.1 V

(b) Induced e.m.f.: e = N × (ΔΦ/Δt) = 200 × 0.1 = 20 V

Rate of change per turn = 0.1 Wb/s; Induced e.m.f. = 20 V.
